`opencode-db-unfuck` (uncorrupts your sqlite):

```sh
#!/bin/bash
bash -c "cd ~/.local/share/opencode && sqlite3 opencode.db '.recover' | sqlite3 opencode.db-recovered && mv opencode.db-recovered opencode.db"
```

**It's not a real solution** but at least if the corruption happens to you you don't need to lose everything and can go back to your previous session and ask the model to continue. It also doesn't work on every type of corruption so if you're very unlucky, well...

> but yeah explicit loop detection just seems like the most straight forward solution to a real problem I've experienced.

I'm not sure I agree... 🤔

once you detect a loop, how do you even mitigate? abort the request, correct it somehow, and then restart? this doesn't sound straight forward to me.

and doesn't practically every model have a "repetition penalty" value you can configure?

wouldn't it make more sense to give us better, more visible model controls? e.g. not floating around in a schemaless area of a JSON blob, no idea what's being picked up or if it's being sent to the provider.

personally, I would invest in something that hardens and surfaces this invisible configuration pipeline, and gives us better control. half the time, I'm not sure if putting anything in that JSON file does anything at all.

in my opinion, we need end-to-end validation, and configuration we can safely edit - actual UI that surfaces the available options.

then we'll be able to turn the knobs provided by the models and experiment - I think we should at least try to address the issue at the root of it, before we start coming up with complex half measures. 🤔

This issue might be a duplicate of existing issues. Please check:
- #8887: Snapshot module ignores `watcher.ignore` config, causing the same `git add .` performance degradation on large files/directories
- #3182: Very slow session due to git snapshots processing large binary/dependency files (same root cause)

Thanks for flagging these — #8887 and #3182 are definitely the same root cause.

#8887 proposes respecting the existing `watcher.ignore` config in the snapshot module, which makes sense as a proactive fix. Our PR (#18069) takes a complementary approach with a runtime safety net: a 15-second timeout on `git add .` that triggers automatic exclude generation only when the operation is actually slow. This handles cases where users haven't configured `watcher.ignore` (which seems common given #3182).

Ideally both approaches could be combined — respect `watcher.ignore` upfront (as #8887 suggests) AND have a timeout fallback for unconfigured workspaces. Happy to update the PR to incorporate the `watcher.ignore` integration from #8887 if the maintainers prefer a combined fix.

Linking: this also fixes #8887 and #3182.

Thanks. This looks related to #15315, but based on our logs it does not appear to be the same failure mode.

What we observed on our side:

- provider: `google`
- reproduced model in the captured logs: `gemini-3-flash-preview`
- this is intermittent, not deterministic

The important difference is that in our case OpenCode does eventually emit the real structured tool part.

From the captured stream:

1. OpenCode first emits a `text` part containing a pseudo narration like:
   ```text
   I'll gather the requested information about the working directory and git branches.

   [tool_call: bash for 'pwd && git branch' because I need to identify the absolute path and list all local branches]
   ```
2. Later in the same turn, OpenCode emits a real `tool` part for the `bash` call.

So the behavior we are seeing is:

- extra plain-text pseudo tool-call narration first
- real structured tool event afterwards

That is why we suspect this issue is related to Gemini tool-calling / transform logic, but not necessarily a duplicate of #15315, which describes a case where structured tool calls are not produced.

If helpful, we can provide a sanitized event sequence showing:

- `message.part.updated` with `part.type=text`
- later `message.part.updated` with `part.type=tool`

So at this point the strongest statement we can make is:

- related to #15315: likely yes
- proven same root cause: not yet

One clarification in case it helps narrow the symptom:

In the affected turns, we are not only seeing text that contains a pseudo `[tool_call: ...]` marker.
We also do see a real structured tool call afterwards in the same turn.

So the observed sequence is specifically:

1. a `text` part whose content includes `[tool_call: ...]`
2. then an actual structured `tool` part is emitted and the tool call really happens

So this is not just "tool call collapsed into text".
It is "textual pseudo tool-call narration appears first, while the real tool call still happens afterwards".

Confirming this on macOS with a local reproduction and concrete cleanup numbers.

Environment
- OS: macOS
- State dir: `~/.local/share/opencode`

What I found locally
- `~/.local/share/opencode` had grown to `45G`
- `snapshot/` was `40G`
- one snapshot dir dominated all usage:
  - `~/.local/share/opencode/snapshot/01adec10548001d548c6d7c392e733d8e7535c65` = `40G`
- inside that snapshot:
  - `objects/pack/` = `39G`
- of that, `tmp_pack_*` files alone accounted for about `19.4 GiB`

Examples from that directory:
- `tmp_pack_MzfB9A` = `15G`
- `tmp_pack_HzAeAw` = `2.9G`
- `tmp_pack_LAQ6cW` = `912M`

Important detail
- these files were not open by any process when I inspected the snapshot dir itself
- deleting only the `tmp_pack_*` files reclaimed about `19-20 GiB` immediately
- the containing snapshot dropped from `40G` to `20G`
- free space on the data volume jumped from about `8.5 GiB` to `28 GiB`

This strongly suggests abandoned/incomplete git repack artifacts are being left behind without cleanup/rollback/GC.

I also had stale leaked `.opencode serve` processes from a separate test issue keeping `opencode.db` open, but those do not explain the `tmp_pack_*` accumulation itself.
This problem urgently needs an official fix, otherwise it will greatly affect the user experience on Windows !

Erratum actually it's working well. On the MCP endpoint, www-authenticate header  should point to his own ressource .well-known/oauth-protected-resource so that opencode can fetch it and discover the actual Oauth server 

Expected response format of your own  .well-known/oauth-protected-resource/<mcp_path>
```
{
  "resource": "https://<your-mcp>/<mcp_path>",
  "authorization_servers": [
    "https://l<your-oauth2-server>"
  ],
  "scopes_supported": [
    "your mcp scope mcp"
  ],
  "resource_name": "whaterver"
}
```
